NCERT + JEE

1.1 Physical Quantities & The International System of Units (SI)

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Physics relies on reproducible quantitative measurement rather than qualitative opinion.
  • By the end of this section, you will classify physical quantities into fundamental and derived types, apply the seven SI base units, and use supplementary angular units (radian and steradian) accurately.

D. Physical Interpretation

A unit is a physical reference scale agreed upon globally. Changing from metres to millimetres does not stretch the object; it multiplies the numerical count by 1000 while shrinking the unit by 1000.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Every physical quantity Q is expressed as the product of a numerical magnitude n and a chosen standard unit u: Q = n u. If the unit is made larger, the numerical value becomes proportionally smaller so that n1 u1 = n2 u2 remains invariant. Seven independent base quantities (length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity) form the bedrock of the SI system.

Level 2 · JEE Main

In the 2019 SI redefinition, all seven base units are anchored to exact invariant physical constants (c,h,e,kB,NA,ΔνCs,Kcdc, h, e, k_B, N_A, \Delta\nu_{\text{Cs}}, K_{\text{cd}}c,h,e,kB​,NA​,ΔνCs​,Kcd​) rather than material artifacts like the platinum-iridium cylinder. Derived quantities are expressed algebraically in terms of base units. Plane angle (radian) and solid angle (steradian) are dimensionless supplementary quantities that still carry distinct geometric units.

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

Any set of linearly independent physical quantities whose dimensional determinant is non-zero can replace {M, L, T} as a valid basis of units (e.g., {G, h, c} in Planck units, or {E, v, F} in mechanics). Note that dimensionless quantities need not be unitless: plane angle in radians and angular velocity in rad/s share dimensions with pure numbers or frequency, yet carry geometric meaning.

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Physical Quantity
Any property of a material or physical system that can be measured directly or indirectly and expressed as a number multiplied by a unit.
Principle of Unit Invariance
The physical magnitude of a quantity is independent of the unit system chosen: Q = n₁u₁ = n₂u₂.
Radian (rad)
The plane angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to its radius (θ = s/r).
Steradian (sr)
The solid angle subtended at the centre of a sphere by a surface patch of area r² (Ω = A/r²).

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Parallax formula D = b/θ assumes the small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ θ (valid when b ≪ D).
  • Coherent SI prefixes scale in powers of 10³, whereas non-SI units such as light-year, parsec, and amu require explicit conversion constants.

I. Schematic Reference

Parallax Angle & Vernier Geometry Reference

Small-angle baseline measurement D = b/θ and instrument scale division alignment.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Unit Conversion Law

n1u1=n2u2  ⟹  n2=n1(M1M2)a(L1L2)b(T1T2)cn_1 u_1 = n_2 u_2 \implies n_2 = n_1 \left(\frac{M_1}{M_2}\right)^a \left(\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right)^b \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^cn1​u1​=n2​u2​⟹n2​=n1​(M2​M1​​)a(L2​L1​​)b(T2​T1​​)c

Valid for all coherent unit systems with exponents a, b, c from the dimensional formula.

Parallax Distance Formula

D=bθD = \frac{b}{\theta}D=θb​

θ must be in radians; b is the baseline (e.g., Earth orbital diameter 2 AU for stellar parallax).

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Length (l) metre (m) [L]
Mass (m) kilogram (kg) [M]
Time (t) second (s) [T]
Electric Current (I) ampere (A) [I]
Temperature (T) kelvin (K) [K]
Plane Angle (θ) radian (rad) [M⁰L⁰T⁰]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • GPS satellite timing synchronization uses atomic cesium clocks ($\Delta\nu_{\text{Cs}}$) accurate to nanoseconds because light travels 30 cm per nanosecond.
  • Astronomical distance ladders measure nearby star distances up to ~100 parsecs using Gaia space observatory parallax.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • 1 parsec = 3.08 × 10¹⁶ m ≈ 3.26 light-years; 1 AU = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m.
  • Order of magnitude of a number N = a × 10^b (with 0.5 ≤ a < 5) has order of magnitude b; if 5 ≤ a < 10, order is b + 1.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Assuming all dimensionless quantities are unitless.

Fix: Angle (rad), solid angle (sr), and relative humidity (%) have zero dimensions [M⁰L⁰T⁰] yet possess well-defined units.

Trap: Inserting degrees directly into s = rθ or D = b/θ.

Fix: Always convert degrees or arcseconds into radians (1″ = 4.848 × 10⁻⁶ rad) before using arc-length formulas.

M. Conceptual Questions

Can a physical quantity have units without dimensions? Give two examples.

Yes. Plane angle (radian) and solid angle (steradian) are ratios of lengths or areas, so their dimensions cancel to [M⁰L⁰T⁰], yet they carry units.

Why is platinum-iridium no longer the official definition of the kilogram?

Physical artifacts drift by tens of micrograms over decades due to surface contamination and cleaning; tying the kg to Planck constant h makes it invariant.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • When asked to create a custom unit system (e.g., Force F, Velocity V, Time T as base), express M = F V⁻¹ T, L = V T, and substitute directly into any target formula.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • Q = n u connects numerical value inversely to unit size.
  • SI defines 7 base units + 2 supplementary geometric units.
  • 1 fermi = 10⁻¹⁵ m, 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
  • Parallax: 1 parsec is the distance where 1 AU subtends 1 arcsecond.
JEE Main & Adv

1.2 Precision Instruments: Vernier Calipers & Screw Gauge

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Ordinary metre scales resolve down to 1 mm; engineering and laboratory experiments require 0.1 mm or 0.01 mm precision.
  • Master least count derivation, positive/negative zero error sign convention, and backlash error prevention.

D. Physical Interpretation

Vernier calipers amplify sub-millimetre gaps visually by noticing which pair of tick marks aligns collinearly, turning a tiny length gap into an easily counted integer index.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

A Vernier Caliper uses a sliding auxiliary Vernier scale alongside a fixed main scale. Because N Vernier Scale Divisions (VSD) match (N − 1) Main Scale Divisions (MSD), each Vernier division is slightly shorter than a main scale division. That small difference is the Least Count (LC).

Level 2 · JEE Main

For a standard Vernier caliper where n VSD = m MSD (usually m = n − 1, though JEE frequently alters m to n − 2 or n + 1!), LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = (1 − m/n) MSD. Total Reading = MSR + (VSR × LC) − Zero Error. Note that if n VSD > n MSD (over-long Vernier), reading rules reverse.

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

In a Screw Gauge (micrometer), Pitch = distance moved per full rotation of the circular head, and LC = Pitch / Number of Circular Scale Divisions. Zero error is positive if the zero of the circular scale lies below the reference datum line when jaws touch, and negative if above it. Always subtract signed zero error: True = Observed − (Signed Zero Error).

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Least Count (LC)
The smallest measurement an instrument can resolve reliably without estimation.
Positive Zero Error
Instrument reads a positive value when jaws are closed; must be subtracted from observed readings.
Backlash Error
Play between screw threads and nut when rotation direction reverses; avoided by rotating the screw in one direction only.

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Assumes uniform thread pitch and zero elastic deformation of jaws under normal ratchet torque.
  • If m > n in a non-standard Vernier problem, divisions on the Vernier exceed 1 MSD and the backward-reading formula must be derived from alignment geometry.

I. Schematic Reference

Vernier Caliper Main Scale & Vernier Alignment

Illustration of MSR + VSR × LC and positive vs negative zero shift.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Vernier Least Count

LC=1 MSD−1 VSD=(1−mn)MSD\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD} = \left(1 - \frac{m}{n}\right)\text{MSD}LC=1 MSD−1 VSD=(1−nm​)MSD

Applies when n VSD = m MSD with m < n.

True Reading with Zero Error

Rtrue=MSR+(ncoincide×LC)−ezeroR_{\text{true}} = \text{MSR} + (n_{\text{coincide}} \times \text{LC}) - e_{\text{zero}}Rtrue​=MSR+(ncoincide​×LC)−ezero​

Keep sign of e_zero (+ for positive zero error, − for negative zero error).

Screw Gauge Least Count

LCsg=PitchNcircular\text{LC}_{\text{sg}} = \frac{\text{Pitch}}{N_{\text{circular}}}LCsg​=Ncircular​Pitch​

If screw advances p mm in k rotations, Pitch = p/k.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Pitch m (commonly mm) [L]
Least Count m (commonly mm) [L]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Machining automotive engine pistons and ball bearings to ±0.01 mm tolerances using digital and mechanical micrometers.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Negative zero error on a screw gauge with N divisions and k-th division above zero line has magnitude −(N − k) × LC.
  • JEE Advanced often mixes non-standard Vernier scales where 10 VSD = 11 MSD.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Adding positive zero error instead of subtracting it.

Fix: Positive zero error means the instrument already shows a head-start reading when closed; subtract it: True = Observed − (+e).

Trap: Taking the circular division k directly as negative zero error.

Fix: If the 96th mark on a 100-division drum aligns with the datum above zero, the error is −(100 − 96) × LC = −4 × LC, NOT −96 × LC.

M. Conceptual Questions

Why does a screw gauge feature a ratchet clutch at the end of the thimble?

To ensure constant, gentle clamping pressure on the specimen so soft wires are not compressed and threads are not strained.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • For any unusual Vernier scale where n VSD = m MSD, write the exact distance from main scale zero to the k-th coinciding mark: x + k·VSD = M·MSD.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD (Vernier) and Pitch / N (Screw Gauge).
  • True Reading = Observed Reading − Signed Zero Error.
  • Check zero error sign carefully before substituting into True = MSR + CSR − e.
NCERT + JEE

1.3 Significant Figures & Error Analysis

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • No physical measurement is exact; every measurement carries an uncertainty interval.
  • You will learn significant figure arithmetic rules, absolute/relative/percentage error propagation, and logarithmic differentiation for JEE problems.

D. Physical Interpretation

Errors never cancel in worst-case engineering design. Even when dividing two quantities A/B, an underestimate of B combined with an overestimate of A pushes the quotient upward—hence relative errors always add.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Significant figures reflect the precision of a measuring device: all reliably known digits plus the first uncertain digit. When adding or subtracting quantities, round to the fewest decimal places. When multiplying or dividing, round to the fewest significant figures.

Level 2 · JEE Main

Measurements of a quantity x repeated n times yield mean x̄ = (1/n)∑x_i and mean absolute error Δx̄ = (1/n)∑|x_i − x̄|. Fractional error is Δx̄/x̄. For a derived quantity Z = A^p B^q / C^r, maximum fractional error adds constructively: ΔZ/Z = |p|(ΔA/A) + |q|(ΔB/B) + |r|(ΔC/C).

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

For general differentiable relations f(x, y) = c (like the lens formula 1/f = 1/v − 1/u or parallel resistance 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂), differentiate implicitly and replace differentials with maximum absolute errors: |Δf|/f² = |Δv|/v² + |Δu|/u². Notice you must NOT apply multiplicative percentage rules across sums or differences directly!

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Accuracy vs Precision
Accuracy measures closeness to the true value; precision measures repeatability and resolution of the instrument.
Systematic Error
Directional bias (instrumental, zero, or environmental) that can be calibrated out once identified.
Random Error
Unpredictable fluctuations around the mean; reduced by taking N repeated readings (error scales as 1/√N).

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Linear differential propagation (ΔZ/Z ≈ dZ/Z) breaks down for large percentage errors (>10%), where exact min/max bounds Z_max − Z_min must be evaluated.

I. Schematic Reference

Error Propagation & Distribution Bounds

Random scatter around true mean and worst-case error envelope.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Power-Law Error Propagation

Z=ApBqCr  ⟹  ΔZZ=pΔAA+qΔBB+rΔCCZ = \frac{A^p B^q}{C^r} \implies \frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = p\frac{\Delta A}{A} + q\frac{\Delta B}{B} + r\frac{\Delta C}{C}Z=CrApBq​⟹ZΔZ​=pAΔA​+qBΔB​+rCΔC​

Assumes independent small errors (ΔA ≪ A); valid up to ~5–10% fractional error.

Sum / Difference Error

Z=A±B  ⟹  ΔZ=ΔA+ΔBZ = A \pm B \implies \Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta BZ=A±B⟹ΔZ=ΔA+ΔB

Absolute errors ALWAYS add even for subtraction A − B.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Absolute Error (Δx) Same as x Same as x
Relative Error (Δx/x) Unitless [M⁰L⁰T⁰]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Bridge and spacecraft structural safety factors combine worst-case tolerances in load, Young’s modulus, and beam cross-sections.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Percentage error in kinetic energy K = p²/(2m): if momentum p changes by 100% (large change!), do NOT use ΔK/K = 2Δp/p; compute (p_new² − p²)/p² = 300%!
  • Rounding off digit 5: if preceding digit is odd, round up; if even, leave unchanged.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Using ΔK/K = 2(Δp/p) when momentum increases by 50% or 100%.

Fix: Differential formulas apply only to small errors (<5%). For large changes, compute exact ratio (1.5² − 1) = 125%.

Trap: Subtracting errors in Z = A − B.

Fix: In Z = A − B, worst-case error is ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB, which can produce a huge percentage error if A ≈ B.

M. Conceptual Questions

Why are trailing zeros in 4.200 m significant while those in 4200 m (without decimal) are ambiguous?

Trailing zeros after a decimal point explicitly show instrument resolution down to the millimetre, whereas integer trailing zeros may only hold place value.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • For implicit relations such as 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂, compute dR/R² = dR₁/R₁² + dR₂/R₂², then multiply through by R to find ΔR/R.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • Absolute errors add for sums/differences; relative errors add (weighted by exponents) for products/quotients.
  • Large percentage changes require exact algebraic evaluation, not differentials.
  • Rule of 5 rounding: Even stays, Odd goes up.
  • Power rule: Δ(xⁿ)/xⁿ = |n|(Δx/x).
Enrichment

1.4 Dimensional Analysis & Buckingham Pi Enrichment

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Dimensions reveal the structural DNA of every physical law.
  • Learn the Principle of Dimensional Homogeneity, derive unknown power-law relations, convert units, and explore the Buckingham Pi Theorem (Enrichment).

D. Physical Interpretation

Dimensional homogeneity guarantees that physical laws remain true regardless of whether an observer measures in SI, CGS, or astronomical units.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Every physical quantity can be written as powers of fundamental dimensions [M^a L^b T^c ...]. Only quantities with identical dimensions can be added, subtracted, or equated—this is the Principle of Homogeneity.

Level 2 · JEE Main

Arguments of transcendental functions (sin θ, cos ωt, e^(-λt), ln(x/x₀)) MUST be completely dimensionless [M⁰L⁰T⁰]. This fact alone lets you deduce dimensions of arbitrary constants inside equations (e.g., α and β in F = α sin(βt)).

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

Buckingham Pi Theorem (Enrichment): If a physical phenomenon involves n dimensional variables built from k independent fundamental dimensions, the system reduces to (n − k) independent dimensionless Π-groups. This explains why dimensional analysis can find T ∝ √(l/g) uniquely (n=3, k=2 ⇒ 1 group) but cannot determine dimensionless constants like 2π or handle additive terms.

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Principle of Dimensional Homogeneity
Every valid physical equation must have identical dimensional formulas on both sides and across every summed term.
Buckingham Pi Theorem (Enrichment)
Any dimensionally homogeneous relation among n variables with k independent dimensions is equivalent to Φ(Π₁, Π₂, ..., Π_{n-k}) = 0.

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Cannot determine pure numerical constants (e.g., 1/2, 2π, 6π).
  • Cannot distinguish between different quantities sharing identical dimensions (e.g., Work vs Torque, or Pressure vs Energy Density).
  • Fails when a formula depends on more than 3 mechanical variables unless extra dimensions (K, A) or dimensionless groups are introduced.

I. Schematic Reference

Dimensional Basis Transformation Matrix

Mapping fundamental dimensions {M, L, T} into arbitrary basis {E, v, T}.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Dimensional Equivalence

[Q]=[MaLbTc][Q] = [M^a L^b T^c][Q]=[MaLbTc]

Equate exponents on LHS and RHS to solve up to 3 independent unknowns (4 with current/temperature).

Transcendental Argument Rule

[ωt]=[M0L0T0]  ⟹  [ω]=[T−1][\omega t] = [M^0 L^0 T^0] \implies [\omega] = [T^{-1}][ωt]=[M0L0T0]⟹[ω]=[T−1]

Applies to all trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic arguments.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Universal Gravitational Constant (G) N·m²/kg² [M⁻¹L³T⁻²]
Planck Constant (h) J·s [M¹L²T⁻¹]
Coefficient of Viscosity (η) Pa·s [M¹L⁻¹T⁻¹]
Surface Tension (σ) N/m [M¹L⁰T⁻²]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Aerospace engineers test scale-model aircraft in wind tunnels by matching the dimensionless Reynolds number and Mach number.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • G, h, c combinations yield Planck Length l_P = √(ħG/c³), Planck Mass m_P = √(ħc/G), Planck Time t_P = √(ħG/c⁵).
  • Van der Waals constants: [a] = [P V²] = [M L⁵ T⁻²], [b] = [V] = [L³].

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Assuming a dimensionally correct equation is physically true.

Fix: s = ut + at² is dimensionally consistent yet misses the factor 1/2. Dimensional correctness is necessary, not sufficient.

M. Conceptual Questions

Why does dimensional analysis fail to derive s = ut + ½at² in one step?

Because dimensional analysis produces only single multiplicative monomials, not sums of distinct terms.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Use exponent matrices and determinants to quickly check if three chosen quantities {X, Y, Z} can serve as a complete mechanical basis.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • Match powers of M, L, T across every term and inside transcendental functions.
  • Dimensional analysis discovers scaling laws up to a dimensionless constant.
  • [Energy] = [Torque] = [M L² T⁻²]; [Stress] = [Pressure] = [Energy density] = [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].
  • [Planck constant h] = [Angular momentum] = [M L² T⁻¹].

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (4)

Unit Conversion Between Arbitrary Systems via Dimensional Formula — Physical magnitude Q is invariant under change of unit size.

Assumptions

  • Both unit systems are coherent and share the same fundamental dimension set {M, L, T}.

Symbols

  • n₁, n₂ — Numerical values in systems 1 and 2 (dimensionless)
  • M₁, L₁, T₁ — Base units of mass, length, time in system 1 (base)
  • a, b, c — Dimensional exponents of the physical quantity (real)

Step 1: State the invariance of physical magnitude.

Q=n1u1=n2u2Q = n_1 u_1 = n_2 u_2Q=n1​u1​=n2​u2​

Step 2: Express both units in terms of their fundamental base dimensions.

u1=M1aL1bT1c,u2=M2aL2bT2cu_1 = M_1^a L_1^b T_1^c, \quad u_2 = M_2^a L_2^b T_2^cu1​=M1a​L1b​T1c​,u2​=M2a​L2b​T2c​

Step 3: Isolate n₂ by dividing both sides by u₂ and grouping identical dimensional bases.

n2=n1u1u2=n1(M1M2)a(L1L2)b(T1T2)cn_2 = n_1 \frac{u_1}{u_2} = n_1 \left(\frac{M_1}{M_2}\right)^a \left(\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right)^b \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^cn2​=n1​u2​u1​​=n1​(M2​M1​​)a(L2​L1​​)b(T2​T1​​)c

Final Result & Physical Significance

n2=n1(M1M2)a(L1L2)b(T1T2)cn_2 = n_1 \left(\frac{M_1}{M_2}\right)^a \left(\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right)^b \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^cn2​=n1​(M2​M1​​)a(L2​L1​​)b(T2​T1​​)c

Allows instant conversion from SI to CGS or custom experimental unit systems without memorizing separate conversion tables.

Worked Example: Convert 1 Newton (SI) into dynes (CGS).

[F] = [M¹ L¹ T⁻²] ⇒ a=1, b=1, c=-2. n₂ = 1 × (1 kg / 1 g)¹ × (1 m / 1 cm)¹ × (1 s / 1 s)⁻² = 10³ × 10² × 1 = 10⁵.

Answer: 1 N = 10⁵ dyne

Least Count of a Generalized Vernier Caliper — Differential scale division mismatch amplifies sub-millimetre offsets.

Assumptions

  • n Vernier scale divisions exactly coincide with m main scale divisions (m < n).

Symbols

  • 1 MSD — Length of one Main Scale Division (mm)
  • 1 VSD — Length of one Vernier Scale Division (mm)
  • LC — Least Count (mm)

Step 1: Equate total lengths of coinciding scale spans.

n (1 VSD)=m (1 MSD)n \,(1\text{ VSD}) = m \,(1\text{ MSD})n(1 VSD)=m(1 MSD)

Step 2: Solve for the length of a single Vernier division.

1 VSD=mn (1 MSD)1\text{ VSD} = \frac{m}{n}\,(1\text{ MSD})1 VSD=nm​(1 MSD)

Step 3: Take the difference between 1 MSD and 1 VSD.

LC=1 MSD−1 VSD=(1−mn)MSD=n−mnMSD\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD} = \left(1 - \frac{m}{n}\right)\text{MSD} = \frac{n - m}{n}\text{MSD}LC=1 MSD−1 VSD=(1−nm​)MSD=nn−m​MSD

Final Result & Physical Significance

LC=(n−mn)MSD\text{LC} = \left(\frac{n - m}{n}\right) \text{MSD}LC=(nn−m​)MSD

Shifting the Vernier jaw by 1 LC moves the 1st Vernier mark into alignment with the next Main Scale mark.

Worked Example: If 20 VSD = 19 MSD and 1 MSD = 1 mm, find the Least Count.

LC = ((20 - 19)/20) × 1 mm = 1/20 mm = 0.05 mm.

Answer: 0.05 mm

Maximum Fractional Error in a Power-Law Physical Quantity — Logarithmic differentiation converts products and powers into linear sums of relative errors.

Assumptions

  • Uncertainties Δa, Δb, Δc are small compared to mean values a, b, c and independent.

Symbols

  • Z — Derived quantity Z = a^p b^q / c^r (varies)
  • Δa, Δb, Δc — Absolute errors in measured quantities (varies)

Step 1: Take natural logarithm on both sides to separate multiplicative factors.

Z=apbqcr  ⟹  ln⁡Z=pln⁡a+qln⁡b−rln⁡cZ = \frac{a^p b^q}{c^r} \implies \ln Z = p\ln a + q\ln b - r\ln cZ=crapbq​⟹lnZ=plna+qlnb−rlnc

Step 2: Differentiate both sides using d(ln u) = du/u.

dZZ=pdaa+qdbb−rdcc\frac{dZ}{Z} = p\frac{da}{a} + q\frac{db}{b} - r\frac{dc}{c}ZdZ​=pada​+qbdb​−rcdc​

Step 3: Replace differentials with finite errors and take absolute signs for worst-case constructive combination.

(ΔZZ)max⁡=∣p∣Δaa+∣q∣Δbb+∣r∣Δcc\left(\frac{\Delta Z}{Z}\right)_{\max} = |p|\frac{\Delta a}{a} + |q|\frac{\Delta b}{b} + |r|\frac{\Delta c}{c}(ZΔZ​)max​=∣p∣aΔa​+∣q∣bΔb​+∣r∣cΔc​

Final Result & Physical Significance

ΔZZ=∣p∣Δaa+∣q∣Δbb+∣r∣Δcc\frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = |p|\frac{\Delta a}{a} + |q|\frac{\Delta b}{b} + |r|\frac{\Delta c}{c}ZΔZ​=∣p∣aΔa​+∣q∣bΔb​+∣r∣cΔc​

Shows that higher-exponent variables dominate uncertainty—precision should be invested first in measuring variables with the largest exponent.

Worked Example: Find % error in kinetic energy K = ½mv² if mass error is 2% and speed error is 3%.

ΔK/K = Δm/m + 2(Δv/v) = 2% + 2(3%) = 8%.

Answer: 8%

Dimensional Derivation of Simple Pendulum Time Period — Principle of Dimensional Homogeneity applied to oscillatory mechanics.

Assumptions

  • Time period T depends only on length l, mass m, and gravitational acceleration g for small oscillations.

Symbols

  • T — Time period of oscillation (s)
  • l — Effective length of pendulum (m)
  • g — Acceleration due to gravity (m/s²)
  • k — Dimensionless proportionality constant (1)

Step 1: Write trial power-law dependence with unknown exponents a, b, c.

T=k la gb mcT = k \, l^a \, g^b \, m^cT=klagbmc

Step 2: Substitute dimensional formulas on both sides.

[M0L0T1]=[L]a[LT−2]b[M]c=[McLa+bT−2b][M^0 L^0 T^1] = [L]^a [L T^{-2}]^b [M]^c = [M^c L^{a+b} T^{-2b}][M0L0T1]=[L]a[LT−2]b[M]c=[McLa+bT−2b]

Step 3: Equate exponents of M, T, and L respectively.

c=0,−2b=1  ⟹  b=−12,a+b=0  ⟹  a=12c = 0, \quad -2b = 1 \implies b = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad a + b = 0 \implies a = \frac{1}{2}c=0,−2b=1⟹b=−21​,a+b=0⟹a=21​

Final Result & Physical Significance

T=klg(experimentally k=2π)T = k\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} \quad (\text{experimentally } k = 2\pi)T=kgl​​(experimentally k=2π)

Proves immediately that time period is independent of bob mass m and scales with the square root of length.

Worked Example: If length of a pendulum is quadrupled, by what factor does T change?

T_new / T = √(4l / l) = 2.

Answer: Doubles (factor of 2)

N. Solved Problem Library (6)

Problem 1 · Basic Conceptual · Principle of unit invariance Q = n₁u₁ = n₂u₂ FOUNDATION

If the unit of length is doubled and the unit of time is halved, what happens to the numerical value of an acceleration of 10 m/s²?

Given: a₁ = 10 m/s² · L₂ = 2 L₁ · T₂ = 0.5 T₁ | Required: Numerical value n₂ in the new system

n2=n1(L1L2)1(T1T2)−2n_2 = n_1 \left(\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right)^1 \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^{-2}n2​=n1​(L2​L1​​)1(T2​T1​​)−2
  1. Write dimensional formula of acceleration: [a] = [L¹ T⁻²].
  2. Substitute L₁/L₂ = 1/2 and T₁/T₂ = 2 into the conversion formula.
  3. n₂ = 10 × (1/2)¹ × (2)⁻² = 10 × (1/2) × (1/4) = 1.25.

Final Answer: 1.25 new units · Strategy: Always keep exponents attached to (old unit / new unit) ratios to avoid inverting factors by mistake.

Problem 2 · Foundation Numerical · Small-angle parallax geometry d = D θ FOUNDATION

A distant planet subtends an angle of 40 arcseconds at an Earth telescope. If the distance to the planet is 6.0 × 10¹¹ m, calculate its diameter.

Given: θ = 40″ · D = 6.0 × 10¹¹ m · 1″ = 4.848 × 10⁻⁶ rad | Required: Diameter d of the planet

d=Dθd = D\thetad=Dθ
  1. Convert angular diameter to radians: θ = 40 × 4.848 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.939 × 10⁻⁴ rad.
  2. Compute d = (6.0 × 10¹¹ m) × (1.939 × 10⁻⁴ rad) = 1.163 × 10⁸ m.

Final Answer: 1.16 × 10⁸ m · Strategy: Never plug degrees or arcseconds directly into arc length formulas; convert to radians first.

Problem 3 · JEE Main · Vernier least count and signed zero error correction JEE MAIN

In a Vernier caliper, 1 MSD = 1 mm and 10 VSD coincide with 9 MSD. While measuring a cylinder diameter, MSR is 2.4 cm, the 6th VSD coincides, and the instrument has a positive zero error of +0.3 mm. Find the true diameter.

Given: 1 MSD = 1 mm · 10 VSD = 9 MSD · MSR = 24 mm · VSR = 6 · e = +0.3 mm | Required: True diameter D

LC=1 MSD−1 VSD\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD}LC=1 MSD−1 VSD
D=MSR+(VSR×LC)−eD = \text{MSR} + (\text{VSR} \times \text{LC}) - eD=MSR+(VSR×LC)−e
  1. Calculate Least Count: LC = 1 mm − (9/10) mm = 0.1 mm.
  2. Compute Observed Reading = 24 mm + (6 × 0.1 mm) = 24.6 mm.
  3. Subtract signed zero error: D = 24.6 mm − (+0.3 mm) = 24.3 mm = 2.43 cm.

Final Answer: 2.43 cm (24.3 mm) · Strategy: Convert MSR to mm before combining with LC in mm, then convert the final result to the requested unit.

Problem 4 · JEE Advanced · Screw gauge least count & negative zero error correction JEE ADVANCED

A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. When jaws touch, the zero of the circular scale is 4 divisions above the reference line. For a wire, the main scale reads 2.5 mm and the 32nd circular division aligns. Find the wire diameter.

Given: Pitch = 0.5 mm · N = 50 · 4 divisions above datum ⇒ negative zero error · MSR = 2.5 mm · CSR = 32 | Required: True wire diameter d

LC=0.550 mm=0.01 mm\text{LC} = \frac{0.5}{50}\text{ mm} = 0.01\text{ mm}LC=500.5​ mm=0.01 mm
d=MSR+(CSR×LC)−ed = \text{MSR} + (\text{CSR}\times\text{LC}) - ed=MSR+(CSR×LC)−e
  1. Find LC = 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm.
  2. Zero line is 4 divisions above datum, so zero error is negative: e = −4 × 0.01 mm = −0.04 mm.
  3. Observed reading = 2.5 mm + (32 × 0.01 mm) = 2.82 mm.
  4. True reading = 2.82 mm − (−0.04 mm) = 2.86 mm.

Final Answer: 2.86 mm · Strategy: Remember: circular zero above datum = negative zero error (subtracting a negative adds the magnitude).

Problem 5 · Multi-Concept · Power-law error propagation JEE MAIN

A physical quantity P is related to four observables a, b, c, d as P = (a³ b²) / (√c · d). The percentage errors in measuring a, b, c, d are 1%, 3%, 4%, and 2% respectively. Find the maximum percentage error in P.

Given: Δa/a = 1% · Δb/b = 3% · Δc/c = 4% · Δd/d = 2% | Required: Maximum percentage error in P

ΔPP=3Δaa+2Δbb+12Δcc+1Δdd\frac{\Delta P}{P} = 3\frac{\Delta a}{a} + 2\frac{\Delta b}{b} + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta c}{c} + 1\frac{\Delta d}{d}PΔP​=3aΔa​+2bΔb​+21​cΔc​+1dΔd​
  1. Write exponents constructively: 3 for a, 2 for b, 1/2 for √c, and 1 for d.
  2. Substitute percentages: 3(1%) + 2(3%) + 0.5(4%) + 1(2%) = 3% + 6% + 2% + 2% = 13%.

Final Answer: 13% · Strategy: Denominator variables still add positively to the maximum uncertainty.

Problem 6 · Challenging Mathematical · Change of dimensional basis JEE ADVANCED

If Energy (E), Velocity (v), and Time (T) are chosen as fundamental physical quantities, find the dimensional formula of Surface Tension (σ).

Given: Fundamental basis = {E, v, T} · Target = Surface Tension σ = Force / Length | Required: Dimensions of σ in terms of [E, v, T]

[σ]=[ExvyTz][\sigma] = [E^x v^y T^z][σ]=[ExvyTz]
  1. Express σ in {M, L, T}: [σ] = [F]/[L] = [M L T⁻²]/[L] = [M¹ L⁰ T⁻²].
  2. Express basis in {M, L, T}: [E] = [M L² T⁻²], [v] = [L T⁻¹], [T] = [T].
  3. Notice σ = Energy / Area = E / L², and since L = v T, we have σ = E / (v T)² = E v⁻² T⁻².
  4. Verify: [E¹ v⁻² T⁻²] = [M L² T⁻²][L⁻² T²][T⁻²] = [M¹ L⁰ T⁻²]. Exact match!

Final Answer: [E¹ v⁻² T⁻²] · Strategy: Often physical identities (like σ = Energy/Area and L = vT) solve basis-change problems in 10 seconds instead of solving 3×3 linear systems.

2.1 Instantaneous Velocity, Acceleration & Calculus Kinematics

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Describing motion accurately requires distinguishing path length (distance) from position change (displacement).
  • Master differential and integral calculus connections between x(t), v(t), and a(t), plus graph area/slope interpretations.

D. Physical Interpretation

Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes, not the direction of motion itself—a ball thrown upward has downward acceleration even while moving upward.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Average speed equals total distance divided by time, whereas average velocity equals net displacement divided by time. When acceleration is constant, three classic kinematic equations link initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a, displacement s, and time t.

Level 2 · JEE Main

Instantaneous velocity is the derivative v = dx/dt (slope of x-t graph), and instantaneous acceleration is a = dv/dt = v (dv/dx). Integrating v(t) gives displacement (signed area under v-t curve), while integrating |v(t)| gives total distance.

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

Non-uniform acceleration problems often express acceleration as a(x) or a(v) rather than a(t). Use the chain rule a = v dv/dx to separate variables cleanly, and inspect turning points where v(t) = 0 to split displacement into distance segments.

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Instantaneous Velocity
v = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt; tangent slope of the position-time curve.
Stopping Distance
Distance travelled under constant deceleration before coming to rest: d_s = u² / (2a).

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Kinematic equations v = u + at and s = ut + ½at² fail if acceleration varies with time or position.

I. Schematic Reference

Velocity-Time Graph & Area-Displacement Correspondence

Slope equals acceleration dv/dt; shaded signed area equals displacement.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Differential Kinematics

v=dxdt,a=dvdt=vdvdxv = \frac{dx}{dt}, \quad a = \frac{dv}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}v=dtdx​,a=dtdv​=vdxdv​

Valid for all smooth 1D motions, uniform or non-uniform.

Constant Acceleration Suite

v=u+at,s=ut+12at2,v2=u2+2asv = u + at, \quad s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2, \quad v^2 = u^2 + 2asv=u+at,s=ut+21​at2,v2=u2+2as

Applies strictly when a is constant in magnitude and direction.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Velocity (v) m/s [L T⁻¹]
Acceleration (a) m/s² [L T⁻²]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Automotive ABS braking distance scales with the square of initial speed (d ∝ u²).

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Distance in nth second: s_n = u + a(n − 1/2).
  • Galileo law of odd numbers: from rest under constant acceleration, distances in equal time intervals follow 1 : 3 : 5 : 7.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Equating distance to magnitude of displacement when velocity reverses sign.

Fix: Find the instant t₀ where v(t₀) = 0 and sum |Δx₁| + |Δx₂| across intervals.

M. Conceptual Questions

Can a body have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration simultaneously?

Yes—at the highest point of vertical throw, v = 0 instantaneously while a = g downward.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Use a = v dv/dx whenever a is given as f(x), and dv/dt = f(v) whenever drag depends on speed.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • Slope of x-t is v; slope of v-t is a; area under v-t is displacement.
  • Average velocity for equal time halves: (v₁+v₂)/2; for equal distance halves: 2v₁v₂/(v₁+v₂).

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Calculus Derivation of Kinematic Equations for Constant Acceleration — Integration of uniform acceleration over time and position.

Assumptions

  • Motion is strictly 1D along x-axis with constant acceleration a.

Symbols

  • u, v — Initial and final velocities (m/s)
  • a — Constant acceleration (m/s²)
  • s — Displacement (m)

Step 1: Integrate a = dv/dt from t = 0 to t.

∫uvdv=∫0ta dt  ⟹  v−u=at  ⟹  v=u+at\int_{u}^{v} dv = \int_{0}^{t} a\,dt \implies v - u = at \implies v = u + at∫uv​dv=∫0t​adt⟹v−u=at⟹v=u+at

Step 2: Substitute v = dx/dt and integrate with respect to time.

∫0sdx=∫0t(u+at) dt  ⟹  s=ut+12at2\int_{0}^{s} dx = \int_{0}^{t} (u + at)\,dt \implies s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2∫0s​dx=∫0t​(u+at)dt⟹s=ut+21​at2

Step 3: Integrate chain-rule identity v dv = a dx.

∫uvv dv=∫0sa dx  ⟹  v2−u22=as  ⟹  v2=u2+2as\int_{u}^{v} v\,dv = \int_{0}^{s} a\,dx \implies \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2} = as \implies v^2 = u^2 + 2as∫uv​vdv=∫0s​adx⟹2v2−u2​=as⟹v2=u2+2as

Final Result & Physical Significance

v=u+at,s=ut+12at2,v2=u2+2asv = u + at, \quad s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2, \quad v^2 = u^2 + 2asv=u+at,s=ut+21​at2,v2=u2+2as

Unifies velocity, time, and displacement under uniform force fields such as near-Earth gravity.

Worked Example: A stone is thrown vertically upward at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Find maximum height and total flight time.

At apex v = 0: 0 = 20² − 2(10)H ⇒ H = 20 m. Time up t_up = 20/10 = 2 s, total T = 4 s.

Answer: H = 20 m, T = 4 s

N. Solved Problem Library (1)

Problem 1 · JEE Main · Turning points where v(t) = 0 reverse motion direction JEE MAIN

A particle moves along the x-axis such that x(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t + 4 (in metres). Find the total distance travelled in the first 4 seconds.

Given: x(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t + 4 · Interval: t ∈ [0, 4] s | Required: Total path length (distance)

v(t)=dxdt=3t2−12t+9v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 3t^2 - 12t + 9v(t)=dtdx​=3t2−12t+9
  1. Factor velocity: v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) = 0 ⇒ turning points at t = 1 s and t = 3 s.
  2. Evaluate positions: x(0) = 4 m, x(1) = 8 m, x(3) = 4 m, x(4) = 8 m.
  3. Sum segment magnitudes: |8 − 4| + |4 − 8| + |8 − 4| = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 m.

Final Answer: 12 m · Strategy: Always check for roots of v(t) = 0 inside the given time window before subtracting endpoints.

3.1 Vector Algebra & Resolution in Orthogonal Axes

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Two- and three-dimensional motion requires decomposing physical quantities into orthogonal unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂.

D. Physical Interpretation

Orthogonal projections allow independent 1D analysis along x, y, and z axes simultaneously.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Vectors carry both magnitude and direction and obey the parallelogram law of addition.

Level 2 · JEE Main

Dot product A·B = AB cos θ extracts projections and tests perpendicularity; cross product A×B = AB sin θ n̂ yields area and torque.

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

In rotating polar frames, unit vectors r̂ and θ̂ vary with angle: dr̂/dt = ω θ̂ and dθ̂/dt = −ω r̂, immediately yielding radial centripetal acceleration −ω²r.

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Unit Vector
A dimensionless vector of magnitude 1 pointing along a specified direction: â = A / |A|.

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Projectile trajectory assumes flat Earth, uniform g, and zero aerodynamic drag.

I. Schematic Reference

Parabolic Projectile Trajectory & Velocity Components

Constant horizontal velocity v_x = u cos θ and uniformly varying vertical velocity v_y.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Parallelogram Resultant

R=A2+B2+2ABcos⁡θR = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}R=A2+B2+2ABcosθ​

Angle θ between tails of A and B.

Projectile Trajectory

y=xtan⁡θ−gx22u2cos⁡2θy = x\tan\theta - \frac{g x^2}{2 u^2 \cos^2\theta}y=xtanθ−2u2cos2θgx2​

Parabolic path in uniform gravity neglecting air drag.

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions

Centripetal Acceleration (a_c) m/s² [L T⁻²]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Ballistic trajectory prediction, river navigation, and satellite dish vector alignment.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Complementary launch angles θ and (90° − θ) yield identical horizontal range R.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Setting speed at maximum height to zero.

Fix: At maximum height, v_y = 0, but horizontal speed v_x = u cos θ remains non-zero.

M. Conceptual Questions

At what angle of projection is horizontal range equal to maximum height?

R = H ⇒ tan θ = 4 ⇒ θ = arctan(4) ≈ 75.96°.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Inclined-plane projectiles: resolve g into g cos β perpendicular to incline and g sin β along incline.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • Horizontal and vertical motions share only time t and remain dynamically independent.
  • R_max = u²/g at θ = 45°; T = 2u sin θ / g; H = u² sin²θ / (2g).

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Equation of Trajectory, Time of Flight, Height, and Range of a Projectile — Independence of perpendicular motions under uniform vertical gravity.

Assumptions

  • Air resistance is negligible and g is constant.

Symbols

  • u — Launch speed (m/s)
  • θ — Launch angle above horizontal (rad)

Step 1: Horizontal acceleration is zero, giving uniform x-motion.

x=(ucos⁡θ)t  ⟹  t=xucos⁡θx = (u\cos\theta)t \implies t = \frac{x}{u\cos\theta}x=(ucosθ)t⟹t=ucosθx​

Step 2: Substitute t(x) into the vertical displacement equation.

y=(usin⁡θ)t−12gt2=xtan⁡θ−gx22u2cos⁡2θy = (u\sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = x\tan\theta - \frac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}y=(usinθ)t−21​gt2=xtanθ−2u2cos2θgx2​

Step 3: Set y = 0 for T and R = u cos θ · T; set v_y = 0 for H.

T=2usin⁡θg,H=u2sin⁡2θ2g,R=u2sin⁡(2θ)gT = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}, \quad H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}, \quad R = \frac{u^2\sin(2\theta)}{g}T=g2usinθ​,H=2gu2sin2θ​,R=gu2sin(2θ)​

Final Result & Physical Significance

y=xtan⁡θ(1−xR)y = x\tan\theta\left(1 - \frac{x}{R}\right)y=xtanθ(1−Rx​)

Compact alternate trajectory equation extremely useful in JEE problems involving clearing walls.

Worked Example: Launch speed u = 50 m/s at 37° (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8), g = 10 m/s². Find T, H, R.

u_x = 40, u_y = 30. T = 2(30)/10 = 6 s; H = 30²/20 = 45 m; R = 40 × 6 = 240 m.

Answer: T = 6 s, H = 45 m, R = 240 m

A projectile crosses two points at the same height h at t = 2 s and t = 6 s. Find the total time of flight and height h (g = 10 m/s²).

4.1 Newton’s Laws, Free-Body Diagrams & Friction

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Translate physical pulley, wedge, and inclined-plane contacts into exact vector force equations.

D. Physical Interpretation

Friction opposes impending or actual relative sliding between contacting surfaces, not necessarily the overall motion of the body.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Net external force equals mass times acceleration (F_net = m a) in an inertial frame. Every action force has an equal and opposite reaction acting on a different body.

Level 2 · JEE Main

Static friction f_s ≤ μ_s N is self-adjusting and matches the tendency of relative slip up to the limiting threshold μ_s N. Once sliding begins, kinetic friction stays nearly constant at f_k = μ_k N.

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

Constraint relations via virtual work (∑ T · a = 0) or string-length differentiation handle movable pulleys cleanly. In accelerating frames of acceleration a₀, add a pseudo-force −m a₀ before applying equilibrium.

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Angle of Repose
Maximum incline angle α before a block slides: tan α = μ_s.
Pseudo Force
Fictitious inertial force F_p = −m a_frame introduced solely in non-inertial frames.

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Ideal strings are massless and inextensible so tension is uniform across frictionless pulleys.

I. Schematic Reference

Free-Body Diagram on Rough Inclined Plane

Resolution of weight mg into mg sin θ and mg cos θ balanced by N and friction f.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Newton Second Law

F⃗net=dp⃗dt=ma⃗\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = m\vec{a}Fnet​=dtdp​​=ma

Mass m constant; for variable mass rockets use F_ext + v_rel(dm/dt) = m dv/dt.

Banked Curve with Friction

vmax⁡=rg(tan⁡θ+μs1−μstan⁡θ)v_{\max} = \sqrt{rg\left(\frac{\tan\theta + \mu_s}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}\right)}vmax​=rg(1−μs​tanθtanθ+μs​​)​

Max safe speed before outward skidding.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Force (F) N (kg·m/s²) [M L T⁻²]
Impulse (J) N·s [M L T⁻¹]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Banked highway curves and conical centrifuge separators.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Maximum friction angle λ = arctan(μ_s) yields minimum pulling force F_min = mg sin λ at angle λ above horizontal.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Assuming static friction always equals μ_s N.

Fix: f_s = μ_s N only at the verge of sliding; below threshold, f_s equals the applied tangential load.

M. Conceptual Questions

Why is it easier to pull a lawn roller than to push it?

Pulling adds an upward vertical component reducing normal force N = mg − F sin θ, hence lowering friction.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Use ∑ T·x = 0 (string virtual work) to relate accelerations across multi-pulley systems in seconds.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • Always isolate each body in an FBD before writing ∑F = ma along chosen axes.
  • Atwood acceleration a = (m₂−m₁)g/(m₁+m₂); Tension T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁+m₂).

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Minimum Force to Pull a Block on a Rough Horizontal Surface — Trade-off between horizontal pulling component and normal-force reduction.

Assumptions

  • Block of mass m rests on horizontal plane with static friction coefficient μ.

Symbols

  • F — Pulling force applied at angle θ above horizontal (N)
  • μ — Coefficient of static friction (1)

Step 1: Vertical force balance.

N+Fsin⁡θ=mg  ⟹  N=mg−Fsin⁡θN + F\sin\theta = mg \implies N = mg - F\sin\thetaN+Fsinθ=mg⟹N=mg−Fsinθ

Step 2: Horizontal threshold condition for impending motion.

Fcos⁡θ=μN=μ(mg−Fsin⁡θ)  ⟹  F=μmgcos⁡θ+μsin⁡θF\cos\theta = \mu N = \mu(mg - F\sin\theta) \implies F = \frac{\mu mg}{\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta}Fcosθ=μN=μ(mg−Fsinθ)⟹F=cosθ+μsinθμmg​

Step 3: Maximize denominator using Cauchy-Schwarz at tan θ = μ.

max⁡(cos⁡θ+μsin⁡θ)=1+μ2  ⟹  Fmin⁡=μmg1+μ2\max(\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta) = \sqrt{1 + \mu^2} \implies F_{\min} = \frac{\mu mg}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}}max(cosθ+μsinθ)=1+μ2​⟹Fmin​=1+μ2​μmg​

Final Result & Physical Significance

Fmin⁡=μmg1+μ2=mgsin⁡λ(tan⁡θ=μ)F_{\min} = \frac{\mu mg}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}} = mg\sin\lambda \quad (\tan\theta = \mu)Fmin​=1+μ2​μmg​=mgsinλ(tanθ=μ)

Pulling horizontally (θ = 0) requires μmg, which is strictly larger than the optimal angled pull.

Worked Example: For m = 10 kg, μ = 3/4, g = 10 m/s², find minimum horizontal-plane pulling force.

sin λ = μ / √(1+μ²) = (3/4)/(5/4) = 3/5. F_min = 10 × 10 × (3/5) = 60 N.

Answer: 60 N

N. Solved Problem Library (1)

Problem 1 · Foundation Numerical · System acceleration and isolated FBD FOUNDATION

Two blocks of masses 4 kg and 6 kg in contact on a smooth horizontal floor are pushed horizontally by a 50 N force applied to the 4 kg block. Find the contact force between them.

Given: m₁ = 4 kg · m₂ = 6 kg · F = 50 N | Required: Normal contact force N between blocks

a=Fm1+m2a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2}a=m1​+m2​F​
N=m2aN = m_2 aN=m2​a
  1. System acceleration a = 50 / (4 + 6) = 5 m/s².
  2. On the 6 kg block alone, horizontal force is N = 6 × 5 = 30 N.

Final Answer: 30 N · Strategy: Treat coupled blocks as one system to get acceleration, then isolate the trailing block for internal contact force.

5.1 Work-Energy Theorem, Potential Energy & Collisions

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Apply work-energy conservation to bypass complex time integrals and analyze collisions with restitution e.

D. Physical Interpretation

Energy accounting converts path-dependent force dynamics into scalar endpoint comparisons.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Work W = ∫ F · dr equals change in kinetic energy ΔK for ALL forces (conservative and non-conservative combined).

Level 2 · JEE Main

Conservative force derives from potential energy via F = −dU/dx. Minima of U(x) correspond to stable equilibrium (d²U/dx² > 0).

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

In a vertical circle of radius R, minimum bottom speed to complete the loop is √(5gR), where tension at top drops to zero while speed at top is √(gR).

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Coefficient of Restitution (e)
Ratio of relative speed of separation to relative speed of approach along the line of impact (0 ≤ e ≤ 1).

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy only before and after impact, not during peak compression.

I. Schematic Reference

Force-Displacement Integral & Potential Energy Well

Work equals area under F(x); equilibrium occurs where dU/dx = 0.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Work-Energy Theorem

Wall=Kf−Ki=12m(vf2−vi2)W_{\text{all}} = K_f - K_i = \frac{1}{2}m(v_f^2 - v_i^2)Wall​=Kf​−Ki​=21​m(vf2​−vi2​)

Holds in inertial frames; include pseudo-force work in non-inertial frames.

Vertical Circle Threshold

vbottom,min=5gRv_{\text{bottom,min}} = \sqrt{5gR}vbottom,min​=5gR​

For a mass on an ideal string; rigid rod requires only √(4gR).

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Work / Energy joule (J) [M L² T⁻²]
Power (P) watt (W) [M L² T⁻³]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Roller-coaster loop design and hydroelectric turbine power calculation P = ρgQH.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Oblique elastic collision of equal masses (one initially stationary) splits outgoing velocities at 90°.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Applying mechanical energy conservation when friction or external push does work.

Fix: Always use W_nc + W_ext = ΔK + ΔU.

M. Conceptual Questions

Why is the minimum speed to loop a vertical circle smaller on a rigid massless rod than on a string?

A rigid rod can exert outward normal support at the top (allowing v_top → 0), whereas a string goes slack unless v_top ≥ √(gR).

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Use centre-of-mass frame in 1D collisions: velocities simply reverse sign multiplied by −e.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • W_total = ΔK universally; F = −∇U for conservative fields.
  • KE loss in inelastic collision: ΔK = ½ [m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂)] (u₁−u₂)² (1−e²).

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Critical Speeds in Vertical Circular Motion (String) — Combined radial centripetal force equation and mechanical energy conservation.

Assumptions

  • Mass m attached to massless inextensible string of length R moving under uniform gravity g.

Symbols

  • v_B, v_T — Speeds at bottom and top of loop (m/s)
  • T — String tension (N)

Step 1: At the highest point, set minimum tension T_top = 0 so string remains taut.

Ttop+mg=mvT2R  ⟹  vT,min⁡=gR(Ttop=0)T_{\text{top}} + mg = \frac{m v_T^2}{R} \implies v_{T,\min} = \sqrt{gR} \quad (T_{\text{top}} = 0)Ttop​+mg=RmvT2​​⟹vT,min​=gR​(Ttop​=0)

Step 2: Apply conservation of mechanical energy from bottom to top (height 2R).

12mvB2=12mvT2+mg(2R)\frac{1}{2}m v_B^2 = \frac{1}{2}m v_T^2 + mg(2R)21​mvB2​=21​mvT2​+mg(2R)

Step 3: Substitute v_T² = gR and take square root.

vB2=gR+4gR=5gR  ⟹  vB,min⁡=5gRv_B^2 = gR + 4gR = 5gR \implies v_{B,\min} = \sqrt{5gR}vB2​=gR+4gR=5gR⟹vB,min​=5gR​

Final Result & Physical Significance

vB,min⁡=5gR,vT,min⁡=gRv_{B,\min} = \sqrt{5gR}, \quad v_{T,\min} = \sqrt{gR}vB,min​=5gR​,vT,min​=gR​

Below √(5gR) and above √(2gR), the bob leaves the circular arc in the upper half and becomes a projectile.

Worked Example: For R = 2 m and g = 10 m/s², find minimum bottom speed to complete the vertical loop.

v_B = √(5 × 10 × 2) = √100 = 10 m/s.

Answer: 10 m/s

N. Solved Problem Library (1)

Problem 1 · JEE Main · Conservation of linear momentum and kinetic energy JEE MAIN

A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on elastically (e = 1) with a stationary 4 kg ball. Find the final velocities of both balls.

Given: m₁ = 2 kg, u₁ = 6 m/s · m₂ = 4 kg, u₂ = 0 · e = 1 | Required: Final velocities v₁ and v₂

v1=m1−m2m1+m2u1v_1 = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}u_1v1​=m1​+m2​m1​−m2​​u1​
v2=2m1m1+m2u1v_2 = \frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}u_1v2​=m1​+m2​2m1​​u1​
  1. v₁ = ((2 − 4)/(2 + 4)) × 6 = (−2/6) × 6 = −2 m/s (rebounds backward).
  2. v₂ = (2 × 2 / 6) × 6 = 4 m/s (moves forward).

Final Answer: v₁ = −2 m/s, v₂ = +4 m/s · Strategy: Verify kinetic energy: initial ½(2)(36)=36 J; final ½(2)(4) + ½(4)(16) = 4 + 32 = 36 J.

6.1 Moment of Inertia, Torque & Pure Rolling Dynamics

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Master rigid body rotation about fixed and translating axes including rolling without slipping.

D. Physical Interpretation

Bodies with mass concentrated near the rim (like rings) store a larger fraction of energy in rotation, making them accelerate slower down inclines.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Moment of inertia I = ∑ m_i r_i² measures rotational inertia just as mass measures translational inertia. Torque τ = r × F produces angular acceleration τ = I α.

Level 2 · JEE Main

Parallel Axis Theorem I = I_cm + Md² applies to all 3D bodies; Perpendicular Axis Theorem I_z = I_x + I_y applies strictly to planar laminas.

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

In general plane motion, angular momentum about any point P is L_P = I_cm ω + M (r_cm × v_cm), and kinetic energy splits cleanly into translational plus rotational parts: K = ½Mv_cm² + ½I_cm ω².

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Pure Rolling Condition
No slip at contact point: v_cm = ωR and a_cm = αR on a stationary surface.

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Pure rolling requires static friction coefficient μ_s ≥ [I/(MR²)] tan θ / (1 + I/(MR²)).

I. Schematic Reference

Rolling Cylinder & Torque Balance on Incline

Static friction at contact creates torque τ = f R driving angular acceleration α.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Rolling Acceleration Down Incline

a=gsin⁡θ1+IcmMR2a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{I_{\text{cm}}}{MR^2}}a=1+MR2Icm​​gsinθ​

Static friction required is f_s = (I_cm / R²) a.

Parallel Axis Theorem

I=Icm+Md2I = I_{\text{cm}} + M d^2I=Icm​+Md2

Axis must be parallel to the CM axis.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Moment of Inertia (I) kg·m² [M L²]
Angular Momentum (L) kg·m²/s [M L² T⁻¹]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Flywheels in automotive engines and figure-skater spin acceleration via I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Instantaneous Axis of Rotation (IAOR) lies at the contact point in pure rolling: K = ½ I_contact ω².

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Applying Perpendicular Axis Theorem I_z = I_x + I_y to a solid sphere or cylinder.

Fix: Perpendicular Axis Theorem holds ONLY for flat 2D planar laminas!

M. Conceptual Questions

Does static friction do work during pure rolling on a stationary ramp?

No—the contact point has zero instantaneous velocity, so friction power f · v_contact = 0.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Angular impulse ∫τ dt = ΔL about the point where impulsive force passes eliminates unknown impulse reactions immediately.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • τ_ext = dL/dt; pure rolling divides energy between ½Mv² and ½Iω².
  • I/(MR²): Solid Sphere = 2/5, Hollow Sphere = 2/3, Solid Disc/Cylinder = 1/2, Ring = 1.

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Acceleration of a Body Rolling Without Slipping Down an Incline — Coupled Newton translational and Euler rotational dynamics under static friction constraint.

Assumptions

  • Rigid symmetric body of mass M, radius R, CM inertia I_cm rolling down incline θ without slip.

Symbols

  • a — CM acceleration down incline (m/s²)
  • f_s — Static friction up the incline (N)

Step 1: Translational Newton law along the incline.

Mgsin⁡θ−fs=MaMg\sin\theta - f_s = MaMgsinθ−fs​=Ma

Step 2: Rotational torque balance about CM combined with pure-rolling constraint α = a/R.

fsR=Icmα=IcmaR  ⟹  fs=IcmR2af_s R = I_{\text{cm}} \alpha = I_{\text{cm}} \frac{a}{R} \implies f_s = \frac{I_{\text{cm}}}{R^2} afs​R=Icm​α=Icm​Ra​⟹fs​=R2Icm​​a

Step 3: Substitute f_s into Step 1 and solve for a.

Mgsin⁡θ=(M+IcmR2)a  ⟹  a=gsin⁡θ1+IcmMR2Mg\sin\theta = \left(M + \frac{I_{\text{cm}}}{R^2}\right)a \implies a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{I_{\text{cm}}}{MR^2}}Mgsinθ=(M+R2Icm​​)a⟹a=1+MR2Icm​​gsinθ​

Final Result & Physical Significance

a=gsin⁡θ1+k2R2a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}}a=1+R2k2​gsinθ​

Independent of mass M and radius R; depends solely on dimensionless shape factor k²/R².

Worked Example: Find acceleration of a solid cylinder rolling down a 30° incline (g = 10 m/s²).

For solid cylinder, k²/R² = 1/2. a = (10 × 0.5) / (1 + 0.5) = 5 / 1.5 = 3.33 m/s².

Answer: 3.33 m/s²

N. Solved Problem Library (1)

Problem 1 · JEE Advanced · Rotational energy conservation JEE ADVANCED

A uniform rod of mass M and length L is pivoted at one end and released from rest from a horizontal position. Find its angular speed ω when it reaches the vertical position.

Given: Rod mass M, length L · I_pivot = ML²/3 | Required: Angular speed ω at bottom

MgL2=12Ipivotω2Mg\frac{L}{2} = \frac{1}{2} I_{\text{pivot}} \omega^2Mg2L​=21​Ipivot​ω2
  1. Centre of mass drops by vertical distance h = L/2.
  2. Equate loss in PE to rotational KE: Mg(L/2) = ½ (ML²/3) ω² ⇒ ω² = 3g/L.

Final Answer: ω = √(3g / L) · Strategy: Pivot reaction does zero work because the pivot point does not move.

7.1 Gravitational Field, Potential, Escape Velocity & Satellites

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Compute fields and potentials inside/outside spherical shells and solve elliptical/circular satellite orbit mechanics.

D. Physical Interpretation

Negative total energy E < 0 signifies a gravitationally bound orbit; E ≥ 0 signifies unbound escape.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Every pair of masses attracts with force F = G m₁ m₂ / r². Surface gravity g = GM/R² decreases with both altitude and depth.

Level 2 · JEE Main

Inside a hollow spherical shell, gravitational field is identically zero and potential is constant at −GM/R. Inside a solid uniform sphere, field grows linearly g(r) = GMr/R³.

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

For elliptical orbits under inverse-square central force, both total energy E = −GMm/(2a) and angular momentum L = m v r sin φ remain conserved simultaneously.

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Escape Velocity
Minimum launch speed from surface to reach infinity with zero residual speed: v_e = √(2GM/R).

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Assumes spherically symmetric mass distribution and neglects atmospheric drag.

I. Schematic Reference

Elliptical Kepler Orbit & Energy Conservation

Planet sweeps equal areas in equal times with speed peaking at perihelion.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Escape & Orbital Speed

ve=2GMR=2gR,vo=GMrv_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}, \quad v_o = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}ve​=R2GM​​=2gR​,vo​=rGM​​

v_e = √2 v_o at the same radius.

Kepler Third Law

T2=4π2GMa3T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} a^3T2=GM4π2​a3

a is the semi-major axis of the elliptical orbit.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Gravitational Potential (V) J/kg [L² T⁻²]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Geostationary communication satellites (T = 24 h at ~35,786 km altitude) and Hohmann orbital transfers.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Total mechanical energy of a circular satellite is E = −K = U/2 = −GMm/(2r).

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Using g_h = g(1 − 2h/R) when height h is comparable to R (e.g., h = R/2).

Fix: Binomial approximation applies only for h ≪ R; otherwise use exact g_h = g R² / (R + h)².

M. Conceptual Questions

Why is total energy of an orbiting satellite negative?

Because potential energy U = −GMm/r outweighs kinetic energy K = +GMm/(2r), keeping the satellite bound.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Use conservation of L (r_p v_p = r_a v_a) and E to solve perihelion/aphelion speeds quickly.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • E = −GMm/(2a); inside hollow shell E_g = 0.
  • Geostationary orbit height ≈ 3.6 × 10⁴ km; Earth v_e = 11.2 km/s.

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Escape Velocity and Total Energy of a Circular Satellite — Conservation of mechanical energy in a conservative central inverse-square field.

Assumptions

  • Zero potential energy reference at r → ∞; negligible air drag.

Symbols

  • M, R — Planet mass and radius (kg, m)
  • v_e — Escape velocity (m/s)

Step 1: Equate total energy at surface to zero energy at infinity.

12mve2−GMmR=0+0\frac{1}{2}m v_e^2 - \frac{GMm}{R} = 0 + 021​mve2​−RGMm​=0+0

Step 2: Substitute GM = gR².

ve=2GMR=2gRv_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}ve​=R2GM​​=2gR​

Step 3: Combine orbital kinetic energy with gravitational potential energy.

Eorbit=K+U=GMm2r−GMmr=−GMm2rE_{\text{orbit}} = K + U = \frac{GMm}{2r} - \frac{GMm}{r} = -\frac{GMm}{2r}Eorbit​=K+U=2rGMm​−rGMm​=−2rGMm​

Final Result & Physical Significance

ve=2GMR,Eorbit=−GMm2rv_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}, \quad E_{\text{orbit}} = -\frac{GMm}{2r}ve​=R2GM​​,Eorbit​=−2rGMm​

Supplying an extra +GMm/(2r) energy unbinds the satellite to infinity.

Worked Example: Find orbital speed near Earth surface given v_e = 11.2 km/s.

v_o = v_e / √2 = 11.2 / 1.414 ≈ 7.92 km/s.

Answer: 7.92 km/s

Problem 1 · JEE Main · Exact inverse-square gravity law JEE MAIN

At what height above Earth’s surface is the acceleration due to gravity reduced to 25% of its surface value?

Given: g_h = 0.25 g | Required: Height h in terms of R

gh=g(RR+h)2g_h = g \left(\frac{R}{R + h}\right)^2gh​=g(R+hR​)2

Final Answer: h = R (≈ 6400 km) · Strategy: Never use 1 − 2h/R when g drops by 75%!

8.1 Stress, Strain, Elastic Moduli & Energy Density

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Quantify deformation resistance of engineering solids and elastic energy stored under load.

D. Physical Interpretation

A stiffer material (higher Y, e.g. steel vs rubber) requires greater stress to produce the same fractional stretch.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Stress is internal restoring force per unit cross-sectional area (F/A); strain is fractional deformation (ΔL/L). Within the proportional limit, Stress = Modulus × Strain.

Level 2 · JEE Main

Elastic energy stored per unit volume is u = ½ × stress × strain = ½ Y ε² = σ²/(2Y). Thermal stress in a clamped rod heated by ΔT is σ_th = Y α ΔT.

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

For a heavy hanging wire under its own weight Mg, total self-elongation integrates linearly varying tension: ΔL = MgL / (2AY).

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Young’s Modulus (Y)
Ratio of tensile/compressive stress to longitudinal strain within Hooke’s limit.
Poisson’s Ratio (σ)
Negative ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain (−Δd/d) / (ΔL/L).

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Hooke’s law holds strictly below the proportional limit; beyond yield point, plastic flow begins.

I. Schematic Reference

Engineering Stress-Strain Curve

Proportional limit, yield point, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Wire Elongation & Energy Density

ΔL=FLAY,u=12Yε2\Delta L = \frac{FL}{AY}, \quad u = \frac{1}{2} Y \varepsilon^2ΔL=AYFL​,u=21​Yε2

Analogous to spring stiffness k_eff = YA/L.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Stress / Young’s Modulus N/m² (Pa) [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]
Strain Dimensionless [M⁰L⁰T⁰]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • I-beam bridge girders maximize bending stiffness per unit mass.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Breaking stress depends ONLY on material, not on wire length or cross-sectional area.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Using u = Y ε² without the factor ½.

Fix: Because stress builds linearly from 0 to σ, average force is ½F, giving u = ½ σε.

M. Conceptual Questions

Why is steel preferred over copper in precision balance springs?

Steel has lower elastic after-effect (hysteresis) and higher Young’s modulus.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Treat elastic rods as springs with k = YA/L in series/parallel combinations.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • Y = FL/(AΔL); u = ½ stress × strain.
  • Isotropic Poisson ratio limits: −1 < σ ≤ 0.5 (metals typically 0.25–0.35).

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Elastic Potential Energy Density in a Stretched Wire — Work done by external stretching force equals stored elastic strain energy.

Assumptions

  • Deformation remains inside the linear Hookean elastic region.

Symbols

  • Y — Young’s modulus (Pa)
  • A, L — Cross-sectional area and natural length (m², m)

Step 1: Express restoring tension at intermediate elongation x.

F(x)=YALxF(x) = \frac{YA}{L} xF(x)=LYA​x

Step 2: Integrate incremental work dW = F dx.

U=∫0ΔLYALx dx=12YAL(ΔL)2U = \int_0^{\Delta L} \frac{YA}{L} x\,dx = \frac{1}{2} \frac{YA}{L} (\Delta L)^2U=∫0ΔL​LYA​xdx=21​LYA​(ΔL)2

Step 3: Divide by volume V = AL.

u=UAL=12Y(ΔLL)2=12×Stress×Strainu = \frac{U}{AL} = \frac{1}{2} Y \left(\frac{\Delta L}{L}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\times\text{Stress}\times\text{Strain}u=ALU​=21​Y(LΔL​)2=21​×Stress×Strain

Final Result & Physical Significance

u=12σε=σ22Yu = \frac{1}{2}\sigma\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma^2}{2Y}u=21​σε=2Yσ2​

Measures energy stored per cubic metre—vital in designing shock absorbers and springs.

Worked Example: Wire L = 2 m, A = 1 mm², Y = 2×10¹¹ Pa stretched by 200 N. Find ΔL.

ΔL = (200 × 2) / (10⁻⁶ × 2×10¹¹) = 400 / 2×10⁵ = 2×10⁻³ m = 2 mm.

Answer: 2 mm

Problem 1 · JEE Main · Thermal expansion constrained by elastic compression JEE MAIN

A uniform metal rod of length L, area A, and Young’s modulus Y is clamped rigidly at both ends and heated by ΔT. Find the compressive thermal force developed.

Given: Length L, area A, Y, α, ΔT | Required: Thermal compressive force F

ε=αΔT\varepsilon = \alpha \Delta Tε=αΔT
F=YAαΔTF = Y A \alpha \Delta TF=YAαΔT
  1. Free thermal strain is αΔT; rigid clamps prevent it, creating compressive stress σ = YαΔT and force F = YAαΔT.

Final Answer: F = Y A α ΔT · Strategy: Notice the force is completely independent of rod length L!

9.1 Hydrostatics, Bernoulli’s Theorem, Viscosity & Surface Tension

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Analyze static fluid pressure, streamlined energy conservation, viscous drag, and capillary meniscus rise.

D. Physical Interpretation

Faster fluid flow in a constriction converts static pressure energy into kinetic energy, causing pressure drop (Venturi effect).

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Static fluid pressure increases with depth: P = P₀ + ρgh. Buoyant upthrust equals the weight of displaced fluid (Archimedes principle).

Level 2 · JEE Main

Along a steady, incompressible, non-viscous streamline, Bernoulli’s equation states P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. Terminal speed of a falling sphere is v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g / (9η).

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

Excess pressure inside a soap bubble with two surfaces is ΔP = 4T/R (vs 2T/R for a liquid drop). Capillary rise is h = 2T cos θ / (ρgr); in insufficient tube length, meniscus flattens to a larger radius R′ without overflowing!

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Surface Tension (T)
Surface energy per unit area or tangential tensile force per unit length along a liquid surface.

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Bernoulli’s equation breaks down in turbulent or strongly viscous boundary flows.

I. Schematic Reference

Venturi & Bernoulli Streamline Constriction

Narrower cross-section increases velocity and reduces piezometer head.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Bernoulli & Continuity

A1v1=A2v2,P+12ρv2+ρgh=constA_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2, \quad P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{const}A1​v1​=A2​v2​,P+21​ρv2+ρgh=const

Steady incompressible irrotational inviscid flow.

Capillary Rise

h=2Tcos⁡θρgrh = \frac{2 T \cos\theta}{\rho g r}h=ρgr2Tcosθ​

θ is contact angle.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Coefficient of Viscosity (η) Pa·s (10 poise) [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹]
Surface Tension (T) N/m (J/m²) [M T⁻²]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Aircraft wing lift, Venturi carburetors, and plant xylem capillary transport.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Coalescence of n identical droplets of radius r releases surface energy ΔE = 4πT(n r² − R²) where R = n^(1/3) r.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Using 2T/R instead of 4T/R for an air-filled soap bubble.

Fix: Soap films have TWO air-liquid interfaces, doubling excess pressure to 4T/R.

M. Conceptual Questions

Why does a liquid not overflow from a capillary tube shorter than its equilibrium rise height?

The meniscus angle increases (cos θ decreases) so curvature flattens until h′ = 2T cos θ′/(ρgr) matches tube height.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • In accelerating containers with acceleration a, effective gravity vector g_eff = g − a tilts equipressure surfaces perpendicular to g_eff.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • P + ½ρv² + ρgh = const; v_efflux = √(2gh).
  • 1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s; Soap bubble ΔP = 4T/R; Drop ΔP = 2T/R.

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Torricelli’s Theorem for Speed of Efflux — Bernoulli’s energy conservation applied from free top surface to exit orifice.

Assumptions

  • Tank area A ≫ orifice area a; fluid is ideal and incompressible.

Symbols

  • h — Depth of orifice below free liquid surface (m)
  • v — Efflux speed (m/s)

Step 1: Both top surface and emerging jet are exposed to atmospheric pressure P₀.

P0+12ρv12+ρgh=P0+12ρv2+0P_0 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h = P_0 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + 0P0​+21​ρv12​+ρgh=P0​+21​ρv2+0

Step 2: Apply A ≫ a approximation and solve for v.

v1=aAv≈0  ⟹  ρgh=12ρv2  ⟹  v=2ghv_1 = \frac{a}{A}v \approx 0 \implies \rho g h = \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 \implies v = \sqrt{2gh}v1​=Aa​v≈0⟹ρgh=21​ρv2⟹v=2gh​

Final Result & Physical Significance

v=2ghv = \sqrt{2gh}v=2gh​

Jet exits with the exact speed a body gains falling freely through height h.

Worked Example: Water exits a small hole 5 m below the open surface (g = 10 m/s²). Find efflux speed.

v = √(2 × 10 × 5) = √100 = 10 m/s.

Answer: 10 m/s

Problem 1 · JEE Main · Volume conservation and Stokes terminal velocity v_t ∝ r² JEE MAIN

A spherical raindrop of radius r falls at terminal velocity 4 m/s. If 8 identical raindrops coalesce into one larger drop, find its new terminal velocity.

Given: v_t1 = 4 m/s · n = 8 drops coalesce | Required: New terminal velocity v_t2

R=n1/3rR = n^{1/3} rR=n1/3r
vt∝r2v_t \propto r^2vt​∝r2
  1. New radius R = 8^(1/3) r = 2r.
  2. Since v_t ∝ r², v_t2 = (2)² × 4 = 16 m/s.

Final Answer: 16 m/s · Strategy: Coalescing scales radius by n^(1/3), hence terminal speed scales by n^(2/3).

10.1 Thermal Expansion, Conduction & Blackbody Radiation

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Analyze thermal expansion of cavities/pendulums, steady heat conduction, and radiative cooling.

D. Physical Interpretation

Heat conduction behaves like Ohm’s law where temperature difference plays the role of voltage.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

Solids expand linearly as ΔL = L α ΔT, in area by β = 2α, and in volume by γ = 3α. Heat transfer occurs by conduction, convection, and electromagnetic radiation.

Level 2 · JEE Main

Steady conductive heat current H = dQ/dt = KA(ΔT/L) obeys exact electrical resistance analogy with thermal resistance R_th = L/(KA).

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

Blackbody peak emission wavelength shifts inversely with absolute temperature (λ_m T = b, Wien’s law), while total radiated power follows Stefan-Boltzmann law P = e σ A T⁴.

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Thermal Resistance (R_th)
Ratio L / (KA) governing steady heat current ΔT / R_th.

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Newton’s law of cooling holds accurately only when excess temperature (T − T₀) ≪ T₀.

I. Schematic Reference

Thermal Expansion & Steady Slab Conduction

Linear temperature gradient across composite series/parallel walls.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Thermal Conduction & Radiation

dQdt=KAΔTL,P=eσA(T4−T04)\frac{dQ}{dt} = \frac{KA\Delta T}{L}, \quad P = e\sigma A (T^4 - T_0^4)dtdQ​=LKAΔT​,P=eσA(T4−T04​)

Temperatures in Kelvin for radiation.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Thermal Conductivity (K) W/(m·K) [M L T⁻³ K⁻¹]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Bimetallic thermostat strips and expansion gaps on steel railway tracks.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Fractional time loss in pendulum clock heated by ΔT: ΔT_clock / t = ½ α ΔT.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Inserting °C into Stefan-Boltzmann T⁴.

Fix: Always convert Celsius to Kelvin (T_K = T_C + 273.15) before raising to the 4th power.

M. Conceptual Questions

Why does water contract when heated from 0°C to 4°C?

Anomalous expansion: open hydrogen-bonded ice-like clusters collapse as temperature rises toward 4°C.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Ice thickness growth on lakes: t ∝ x² because heat conducts through growing ice layer x.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • γ = 3α; R_th = L/(KA); P = eσAT⁴; λ_m T = const.
  • Series slabs add R_th; parallel slabs add 1/R_th.

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Effective Thermal Conductivity of Two Slabs in Series — Conservation of steady-state heat current across series interfaces.

Assumptions

  • Two slabs of equal area A, thicknesses L₁, L₂, conductivities K₁, K₂ with insulated sides.

Symbols

  • H — Steady heat current dQ/dt (W)

Step 1: Sum thermal resistances in series.

Req=R1+R2=L1K1A+L2K2AR_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 = \frac{L_1}{K_1 A} + \frac{L_2}{K_2 A}Req​=R1​+R2​=K1​AL1​​+K2​AL2​​

Step 2: Equate total thermal resistance and solve for K_eq.

L1+L2KeqA=L1K1A+L2K2A  ⟹  Keq=L1+L2L1K1+L2K2\frac{L_1 + L_2}{K_{\text{eq}} A} = \frac{L_1}{K_1 A} + \frac{L_2}{K_2 A} \implies K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{L_1 + L_2}{\frac{L_1}{K_1} + \frac{L_2}{K_2}}Keq​AL1​+L2​​=K1​AL1​​+K2​AL2​​⟹Keq​=K1​L1​​+K2​L2​​L1​+L2​​

Final Result & Physical Significance

Keq=L1+L2L1K1+L2K2K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{L_1 + L_2}{\frac{L_1}{K_1} + \frac{L_2}{K_2}}Keq​=K1​L1​​+K2​L2​​L1​+L2​​

For equal thicknesses, K_eq reduces to the harmonic mean 2K₁K₂/(K₁+K₂).

Worked Example: Copper rod L = 1 m, α = 1.7×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ heated by ΔT = 100 K. Find ΔL.

ΔL = 1 × 1.7×10⁻⁵ × 100 = 1.7×10⁻³ m = 1.7 mm.

Answer: 1.7 mm

N. Solved Problem Library (1)

Problem 1 · JEE Main · Newton’s law of cooling (average temperature form) JEE MAIN

A body cools from 60°C to 50°C in 10 minutes in surroundings at 25°C. Estimate the time to cool from 50°C to 40°C.

Given: T₀ = 25°C · 60→50°C in 10 min | Required: Time for 50→40°C

T1−T2t=K(T1+T22−T0)\frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = K\left(\frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)tT1​−T2​​=K(2T1​+T2​​−T0​)
  1. (60−50)/10 = K(55 − 25) ⇒ 1 = 30 K ⇒ K = 1/30 min⁻¹.
  2. (50−40)/t = (1/30)(45 − 25) = 20/30 = 2/3 ⇒ t = 15 min.

Final Answer: 15 minutes · Strategy: Average-temperature Newton cooling avoids logarithms cleanly in JEE problems.

11.1 First Law, Thermodynamic Processes & Carnot Cycle

A. Introduction & Learning Objectives

  • Compute ΔQ, ΔU, and W across P-V cycles and evaluate Carnot engine/refrigerator efficiencies.

D. Physical Interpretation

Internal energy U is a path-independent state function, whereas heat Q and work W depend on the exact thermodynamic path.

B. Theoretical Explanation

Level 1 · Foundation Physics

The First Law ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW expresses energy conservation: heat supplied increases internal energy and performs boundary expansion work.

Level 2 · JEE Main

For ideal gases, ΔU = n C_v ΔT depends ONLY on temperature change for EVERY process! Work W = ∫ P dV equals the signed area under the P-V curve.

Level 3 · JEE Advanced

For a general polytropic process P V^x = constant, molar heat capacity is C = C_v + R/(1 − x). Adiabatic curves (P V^γ = const) are steeper than isothermal curves by factor γ.

C. Definitions & Fundamental Principles

Mayer’s Relation
C_p − C_v = R for 1 mole of any ideal gas.

G. Assumptions & Limitations

  • Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_C/T_H is an absolute upper bound only for reversible cycles.

I. Schematic Reference

P-V Carnot Cycle & Isothermal vs Adiabatic Slopes

Clockwise closed loop yields positive net work equal to enclosed area.

E. Mathematical Formulation

Isothermal & Adiabatic Work

Wiso=nRTln⁡(V2V1),Wad=P1V1−P2V2γ−1W_{\text{iso}} = nRT\ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right), \quad W_{\text{ad}} = \frac{P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2}{\gamma - 1}Wiso​=nRTln(V1​V2​​),Wad​=γ−1P1​V1​−P2​V2​​

Ideal gas processes.

H. SI Units & Dimensional Formulae

Physical Quantity SI Unit Dimensions
Molar Gas Constant (R) J/(mol·K) [M L² T⁻² mol⁻¹ K⁻¹]

J. Real-Life Applications

  • Internal combustion Otto/Diesel cycles and vapor-compression air conditioners.

K. Important Exam Concepts

  • Free expansion into vacuum: Q = 0, W = 0 ⇒ ΔU = 0 ⇒ temperature of an ideal gas stays constant.

L. Common Mistakes & Fixes

Trap: Computing ΔU = n C_p ΔT during an isobaric process.

Fix: Internal energy is ALWAYS ΔU = n C_v ΔT regardless of process; n C_p ΔT is the heat ΔQ at constant pressure!

M. Conceptual Questions

Why is the slope of an adiabatic curve steeper than an isotherm at the same P-V point?

(dP/dV)_ad = −γ(P/V) whereas (dP/dV)_iso = −(P/V), and γ > 1.

O–Q. Advanced Techniques, Summary & Revision

Advanced Strategy

  • Convert V-T or P-T graphs into P-V loops first to determine sign of net work quickly.

Summary & Revision Notes

  • ΔQ = ΔU + W; ΔU = nC_vΔT always; η_Carnot = 1 − T_C/T_H.
  • Adiabatic: PV^γ = const, TV^(γ−1) = const; Polytropic C = C_v + R/(1−x).

F. Mathematical Derivation Engine (1)

Work Done in Reversible Adiabatic Expansion — First law with ΔQ = 0 and adiabatic equation of state P V^γ = K.

Assumptions

  • n moles of ideal gas expanding quasi-statically without heat exchange.

Symbols

  • γ — Adiabatic index C_p / C_v (1)

Step 1: Substitute P = K V^(−γ).

W=∫V1V2P dV=K∫V1V2V−γ dVW = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,dV = K \int_{V_1}^{V_2} V^{-\gamma}\,dVW=∫V1​V2​​PdV=K∫V1​V2​​V−γdV

Step 2: Use K = P₁V₁^γ = P₂V₂^γ and ideal gas law.

W=K(V21−γ−V11−γ)1−γ=P1V1−P2V2γ−1=nR(T1−T2)γ−1W = \frac{K(V_2^{1-\gamma} - V_1^{1-\gamma})}{1 - \gamma} = \frac{P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}W=1−γK(V21−γ​−V11−γ​)​=γ−1P1​V1​−P2​V2​​=γ−1nR(T1​−T2​)​

Final Result & Physical Significance

Wad=nR(T1−T2)γ−1W_{\text{ad}} = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}Wad​=γ−1nR(T1​−T2​)​

Expansion work comes directly from cooling internal energy: W = −ΔU.

Worked Example: Find isothermal work when 2 mol of ideal gas at 300 K doubles in volume (ln 2 ≈ 0.693).

W = 2 × 8.314 × 300 × 0.693 ≈ 3457 J.

Answer: 3457 J

N. Solved Problem Library (1)

Problem 1 · JEE Main · Isobaric ratio W / ΔQ = R / C_p JEE MAIN

A monoatomic ideal gas undergoes an isobaric expansion doing 100 J of work. Find the heat absorbed by the gas.

Given: Monoatomic γ = 5/3, C_p = 5R/2 · W = 100 J | Required: Heat absorbed ΔQ

W=nRΔT,ΔQ=nCpΔTW = nR\Delta T, \quad \Delta Q = n C_p \Delta TW=nRΔT,ΔQ=nCp​ΔT
  1. Since C_p = (5/2)R, ΔQ = (5/2) nR ΔT = 2.5 W = 2.5 × 100 = 250 J.

Final Answer: 250 J · Strategy: In any isobaric process, fraction of heat turned into work is 1 − 1/γ = 2/5.
